outcome: Still open as of 11 October 2026: no accepted existence or nonexistence result. Since 26 January 2024 there are three partial structural papers (Smith and Montemanni, Symmetry, November 2024; Smith and Montemanni, Axioms, May 2026; Ishida, arXiv, June 2026, which shows any such graph would have no involutory automorphisms), and no event that settles the question. The two nonexistence claims (Yang and Zhu, arXiv, October 2019; Makhnev, arXiv, October 2020) are unrefereed preprints that Faber and Keegan disputed in 2022 and that later sources still treat as open.
problem_asks: Single question: does a Moore graph with girth 5 and degree 57 exist (answer yes or no)? Unpacked: (a) a 57-regular graph with girth 5, i.e. no cycles of length 3 or 4; (b) existence of such a graph, which by the Moore bound forces diameter 2 and 3250 = 57^2 + 1 vertices, and makes it a strongly regular graph with parameters (3250, 57, 0, 1). The statement does not ask for uniqueness, the automorphism group, a construction, or a nonexistence proof; those are discussed in the literature as related or partial questions and are recorded below only where events bear on them. The degree 2, 3 and 7 cases (5-cycle, Petersen graph, Hoffman-Singleton graph) are known and are not part of what is asked.

events.what_happened: A. J. Hoffman and R. R. Singleton, 'On Moore Graphs with Diameters 2 and 3', IBM Journal of Research and Development 4 (1960), 497-504. Spectral argument that a diameter-2 Moore graph has degree 2, 3, 7 or 57; the degrees 2, 3, 7 are realised (pentagon, Petersen graph, Hoffman-Singleton graph); degree 57 is left undecided. Known from the Wikipedia article and search summaries of the scan; the scan itself was not opened.
events.delivers: Reduces the diameter-2 case to degrees 2, 3, 7, 57. Settles degrees 2, 3, 7 (existence and uniqueness). Says nothing either way about degree 57.
events.remains: Existence (and uniqueness) for degree 57, which is the whole question.

checked_by.who: IBM Journal of Research and Development (publisher of the 1960 note)
checked_by.qualification: Journal of record; its refereeing practice in 1960 was not checked

events.directly_checkable: The degree 2, 3, 7 graphs are checkable by hand; degree 57 is not an object that has been exhibited.
events.direction: Partial reduction. For degree 57 it leaves the question open and cuts neither way.

events.what_happened: R. M. Damerell, 'On Moore Graphs', Proc. Cambridge Philosophical Society 74 (1973), 227-236; and E. Bannai and T. Ito, 'On finite Moore graphs', J. Fac. Sci. Univ. Tokyo Sect. I A 20 (1973), 191-208. Independently show that there are no Moore graphs of diameter 3 or more with degree 3 or more, apart from odd cycles. Read from the Wikipedia article (opened) and MathWorld search summary (not opened). Titles differ between sources for the Bannai-Ito paper.
events.delivers: Excludes every Moore graph of diameter 3 or more (degree 3 or more). Diameter 2 is untouched, so degree 57 is not addressed.
events.remains: The diameter-2 case, including degree 57, which is the whole question.
events.direction: Neutral for degree 57: it covers other diameters only.

events.what_happened: Structural restrictions on a hypothetical degree-57 diameter-2 Moore graph Gamma: Aschbacher showed it cannot have rank 3 (so it is not distance-transitive); a result that it cannot be vertex-transitive. The Makhnev-Paduchikh 2001 abstract (opened) credits the vertex-transitivity result to Cameron; Dalfo (2019) and Ishida (2026) credit Higman, whose argument Ishida describes as an older unpublished one, extending Aschbacher's work. The earliest appearance found is a Cameron citation dated 1983, cited on the Tjapko problem page (not opened). The date of Aschbacher's rank-3 result was not found; it must be no later than 2001, the date of the abstract that cites it.
events.delivers: If a degree-57 Moore graph exists, it is not vertex-transitive and not of rank 3. These restrict any graph that exists; they say nothing about whether one exists.
events.remains: Existence of the graph, which is the whole question.
events.direction: Restricts the symmetry of any hypothetical graph. Neither for nor against existence.

events.what_happened: A. A. Makhnev and D. V. Paduchikh, 'Automorphisms of Aschbacher Graphs', Algebra i logika 40(2) (2001), 125-134. The abstract (opened) studies fixed-point subgraphs of automorphisms of a hypothetical degree-57 Moore graph, and the structure of its automorphism group under the assumption that the group contains an involution. The 2009 follow-up (Makhnev and Paduchikh) and a bound of 550 for even order are reported only in search summaries; the 550 figure was not in the 2001 abstract I read.
events.delivers: Restrictions on the automorphism group of a hypothetical degree-57 Moore graph, under the involution assumption. Bounds are not stated in the abstract. No existence result.
events.remains: Existence of the graph; the even-order case under this route.

checked_by.qualification: Refereed Russian algebra journal; refereeing not verified

events.direction: Restricts symmetry under an assumption; neither for nor against existence.

events.what_happened: M. Mačaj and J. Širáň (2010 per the reference list of Ishida 2026) bound the automorphism group of any hypothetical degree-57 Moore graph: order at most 375 if the order is odd and at most 110 if it is even. Stated in Ishida's introduction (opened, HTML) and in Dalfó 2019 and the Wikipedia article (opened). The journal and full text were not opened. One search summary gives 275 for the odd case; Ishida's HTML shows '375375' and '110110', which looks like a rendering artefact. The 375 and 110 figures are the ones the sources I opened agree on.
events.delivers: Upper bounds on |Aut|: at most 375 (odd order), at most 110 (even order). No existence result.
events.remains: Existence, and the exact automorphism group if the graph exists.
events.doubts: Only secondary statements of the bound were read; the 275 figure in one search summary conflicts with 375 and was not resolved.
events.direction: Restricts symmetry; neither for nor against existence.

events.what_happened: Joshua E. Ducey, 'On the critical group of the missing Moore graph', arXiv:1509.00327, submitted 1 September 2015, v2 6 October 2016. Abstract (opened) proves that all Sylow p-subgroups of the critical group are elementary abelian except for p = 5, and that the 5-rank of the Laplacian determines the critical group up to two possibilities. Treats the graph as hypothetical. A search summary reports the eigenvalue multiplicities 1729 (for 7) and 1520 (for -8); not confirmed in the abstract.
events.delivers: Constraints on the critical group, and so the Smith normal form of the Laplacian, of a hypothetical degree-57 Moore graph. Conditional on existence. Does not establish existence or uniqueness.
events.remains: Existence and uniqueness; the critical group itself is only constrained, not determined.
events.direction: Neutral; constraints on a hypothetical graph.

events.what_happened: Xu Yang and Xiao-Min Zhu, 'The missing Moore graph is really missing', arXiv:1910.05989, October 2019. The title and abstract were read at www.arxiv.org/abs/1910.05989v1. The abstract introduces a 'fractal block design', a generalisation of block designs inspired by the geodetic properties of Moore graphs, and states: 'As a result, we make sure that the missing Moore graph of degree 57 does not exist.' The argument itself was not read. IDENTITY CONFLICT: arxiv.org/abs/1910.05989 and export.arxiv.org return a different paper with the same ID (Zhu and Yang, 'The classification of local m-GCI-group on finite nonabelian simple groups', v1 14 Oct 2019, v2 15 Oct 2019). The 14 and 15 October dates therefore belong to that other paper and are not used here; the month is taken from the arXiv identifier prefix (1910).
events.revisions: Day of v1 and any later versions of the Moore-titled paper not verified because of the identity conflict.
events.delivers: Claims the full result: no degree-57 Moore graph exists, via the fractal block design argument. Argument not read, so the claim's scope and any restriction it carries are unknown.
events.remains: Nothing, if the claim holds; otherwise existence, which is the whole question.
events.doubts: No journal publication found. Faber and Keegan (2022) discuss the Makhnev claim, not this one, in the parts I read. Epoch AI (2026), Wikipedia and Ishida (2026) all describe the problem as open. The authors' qualifications were not verified. Search summaries describe the claim as not accepted; I did not verify that.
events.direction: Claims nonexistence, which cuts against existence.

events.what_happened: A. A. Makhnev, 'Moore graph with parameters (3250,57,0,1) does not exist', arXiv:2010.13443, v1 26 October 2020, v2 9 November 2020; math.CO; 7 pages, in Russian. Abstract (opened): using the Jurisic-Vidali equivalence (a Moore graph of degree k > 3 exists iff a distance-regular graph with intersection array {k-2, k-3, 2; 1, 1, k-3} exists), it proves that no distance-regular graph with intersection array {55, 54, 2; 1, 1, 54} exists, and so no degree-57 Moore graph exists. The case analysis is not in the abstract. No journal reference on the arXiv page. A journal publication was not found; Algebra i logika 59(4) (2020) by Makhnev and Paduchikh with the same array is an automorphism study and is recorded separately as a discarded event.
events.delivers: Claims the full result: no degree-57 Moore graph exists, by showing the distance-regular graph with array {55,54,2;1,1,54} does not exist. Scope of the claim is the whole question if the reduction and the case analysis are sound.
events.remains: Nothing, if the claim holds; otherwise existence.

checked_by.qualification: arXiv authors in math.CO; their qualifications were not verified in the sources I read
checked_by.what_they_did: Publicly challenged the case analysis: the equation system 'factors into small diagonal blocks all of which have solutions', so the claim 'seems not to be correct'. They do not claim a full refutation.

events.time_since_posted: about 6 years, no journal version found
events.doubts: Faber and Keegan (2022) identify a specific step, the case analysis, as seemingly wrong, and I found no answer to it in the sources I read. Preprint only; no journal reference found. The 2026 Ishida preprint and the Smith and Montemanni 2026 abstract both treat the problem as open. Ishida's introduction, as summarised from the HTML, mentions Makhnev-Paduchikh (2001, 2009) but not this 2020 claim.
events.direction: Claims nonexistence, which cuts against existence.

events.what_happened: A. A. Makhnev and D. V. Paduchikh, 'The largest Moore graph and a distance-regular graph with intersection array {55,54,2;1,1,54}', Algebra i logika 59(4) (2020), 471-479. The one-sentence abstract (opened) says only that the authors point out possible automorphisms of a distance-regular graph with that array and spectrum 55^1, 7^1617, -1^110, -8^1408. It does not state a nonexistence result. A search summary attributed the nonexistence of this graph to this paper; the abstract does not support that. The full text was not read.
events.delivers: As read: possible automorphisms of a hypothetical distance-regular graph with the array; no existence or nonexistence result for it or for the degree-57 Moore graph.
events.remains: Existence of the degree-57 Moore graph; existence of the distance-regular graph with that array.
events.direction: Neutral as read. Discarded because the abstract does not state a result on existence.

events.what_happened: Paul Renteln, 'Some constraints on the missing Moore graph', Australasian Journal of Combinatorics 77(3) (2020), 373-382; received 22 September 2019. The landing page (opened) gives the abstract 'We derive some constraints on the structure of the missing Moore graph'; a search summary adds that the constraints concern the adjacency matrix. The PDF returned unreadable binary and was not read. No arXiv or other preprint was found; the first public version may be earlier than the volume date.
events.revisions: Received 2019-09-22; volume dated June 2020. Earlier public version not identified.
events.delivers: Constraints on the structure of any degree-57 Moore graph; the constraints themselves were not read. No existence result is stated in the abstract.
events.remains: Existence, and the full structure if the graph exists.

checked_by.who: Australasian Journal of Combinatorics (journal of record)
checked_by.qualification: Refereed combinatorics journal; refereeing of this paper not verified

events.direction: Restricts structure; neither for nor against existence.

events.what_happened: Vance Faber and Jonathan Keegan, 'Existence of a Moore graph of degree 57 is still open', arXiv:2210.09577, math.CO. Abstract (opened, partly quoted): it notes the 2020 arXiv claim (Makhnev); says the case analysis 'seems not to be correct' because the system of equations 'factors into small diagonal blocks all of which have solutions'; and reformulates existence in terms of a family of permutation systems, with the graph existing iff some member of the family has no solutions. Title says existence remains open. No journal reference found.
events.delivers: Neither existence nor nonexistence. Challenges the Makhnev case analysis as seemingly incorrect, and reformulates existence as a permutation-system question. Restriction: a reformulation and an objection, not a proof.
events.doubts: The objection is stated as 'seems not to be correct', and the authors do not claim a full refutation. No independent public engagement with their objection was found.
events.direction: Disputes a nonexistence claim; leaves existence open.

events.what_happened: C. Dalfó, 'A survey on the missing Moore graph', Linear Algebra and its Applications 569 (2019), 1-14, DOI 10.1016/J.LAA.2018.12.035. Per a search summary of the abstract (not read directly; the portal page and the DOI redirect gave metadata only), it reviews known properties of a hypothetical degree-57 diameter-2 graph and adds new results: when the distance partition is induced by a set C of 400 independent vertices, several graphs are distance-regular, including the subgraph induced on distance-1 vertices and the line graph; the graph is edge-distance-regular. The DOI's acceptance date suggests the first online version may be from December 2018.
events.delivers: Survey plus new structural results about a hypothetical degree-57 graph. No existence or nonexistence result.
events.remains: Existence, which is the whole question.
events.direction: Neutral; structural results only.

events.what_happened: Derek H. Smith and Roberto Montemanni, 'The missing Moore graph as an optimization problem', EURO Journal on Computational Optimization 11 (2023), article 100060; listed as January 2023 on DOAJ. Recasts existence as an optimisation problem. Their algorithm's solutions contain far fewer edges than a degree-57 graph would need; the authors say this points towards nonexistence and offer the problem as a test-bed for optimisation algorithms. Per the search summary this is evidence, not proof. The DOAJ and journal pages returned 403, so this is from a search summary only and was not opened. The algorithm is described as an optimisation method, not as AI.
events.delivers: Computational evidence against existence (heuristic). Not a proof of nonexistence.
events.remains: Existence, and the nonexistence that the evidence points to.
events.doubts: Heuristic evidence; the authors themselves present it as suggestive, not conclusive (per summary).
events.direction: Heuristic evidence leaning towards nonexistence; no proof.

events.what_happened: Derek H. Smith and Roberto Montemanni, 'Potential Subgraphs of the Missing Moore Graph', Symmetry 16(12) (2024), 1563. Received 16 Oct 2024, revised 11 Nov 2024, accepted 18 Nov 2024, published 22 Nov 2024 (from search summaries; the PDF and MDPI page returned 403, so this was not opened). Assumes a cyclic group of permutations, builds a constraint model for 't-subgraphs', and solves it with Google OR-Tools CP-SAT. Per the summary it constructs larger potential t-subgraphs than previously known (20 subgraphs against 15 previously known), and extends a construction of mutually orthogonal Latin rectangles. A full set of 57 such subgraphs would imply existence of the graph. CP-SAT is a constraint solver, not recorded here as an AI system.
events.revisions: Received 16 Oct 2024; revised 11 Nov 2024; accepted 18 Nov 2024; published 22 Nov 2024. No preprint found.
events.delivers: Partial structures (potential t-subgraphs) under a cyclic-group assumption: 20 subgraphs, per the summary, against the 57 a full structure would need. Neither existence nor nonexistence.
events.remains: Existence; a full set of 57 such subgraphs, which the summary says would imply existence.
events.directly_checkable: A t-subgraph is checkable from its adjacency structure, but the constructions were not read.
events.direction: Toward existence in the sense of building partial structure; not a resolution.
events.object: Potential t-subgraphs of a hypothetical degree-57 Moore graph, built under a cyclic-permutation model: 20 subgraphs per the summary, against 15 previously known. These are partial structures, not the complete graph. Explicit construction details were not read.

events.what_happened: Derek H. Smith and Roberto Montemanni, 'The Moore Graph of Diameter 2 and Degree 57 via Cyclic Derangements', Axioms 15(5) (2026), article 332. Received 6 Feb 2026, revised 8 Apr 2026, accepted 27 Apr 2026, published 1 May 2026 (from search summaries; the PDF and MDPI page returned 403, so this was not opened). Per the summary, the approach encodes adjacencies between leaf vertices as derangements, and the main result is negative for one route: a construction using only a cyclic group of derangements is impossible. It leaves other groups of derangements, or derangement sets that are not groups, open. The abstract describes the question as open for over 65 years. One search summary also says the paper states the evidence strongly suggests nonexistence but a proof is still needed; this is unverified.
events.revisions: Received 6 Feb 2026; revised 8 Apr 2026; accepted 27 Apr 2026; published 1 May 2026. No preprint found.
events.delivers: Rules out one construction route, cyclic groups of derangements. Neither existence nor nonexistence of the graph.
events.remains: Existence, and the other routes (other groups of derangements, non-group derangement sets).
events.doubts: Read from a summary, not the paper. The summary's 'nonexistence strongly suggested' statement is unverified and should not be relied on until the paper is read.
events.direction: A negative result about one construction route; neither for nor against existence of the graph.

events.what_happened: Yawara Ishida, 'No involutions in the missing Moore graph', arXiv:2606.29183, math.CO; single author; affiliation given as 'A.I. System Research, Inc., Kyoto, Japan'. v1 Sunday 28 June 2026; v2 8 July 2026 (current). Theorem 1.1 (per the HTML fetch): a Moore graph of diameter two and degree 57 has no automorphism of order 2, so its automorphism group has odd order (Corollary 6.1). The introduction says the main result 'eliminates the even-order case altogether'. Method (abstract): a trace-rank identity from Brauer quotients of p-permutation lattices, applied to the 2-adic summand for eigenvalue -8, giving a contradiction. Read: the arXiv abstract page and the HTML version (first 100,000 of 100,069 characters). The PDF returned unreadable binary.
events.revisions: v1 28 Jun 2026; v2 8 Jul 2026 (current). v1 and v2 differences not examined.
events.delivers: Structural only: any degree-57 Moore graph has odd-order automorphism group, with no involutions. This removes the even-order branch that the 110 bound (Mačaj-Širáň) and the Makhnev-Paduchikh route had covered. It does not establish existence or nonexistence.
events.remains: Existence. The odd-order case, which keeps the 375 bound, is also open.
events.direction: A restriction on symmetry of any hypothetical graph, which narrows structure without deciding existence.

events.what_happened: Ryosuke Mizuno, 'New lower bounds for the degree/diameter problem via interaction with a browser-accessible LLM', arXiv:2606.15860, math.GM, v1 14 June 2026. Abstract (opened) gives graphs showing N(12,5) >= 34,992 and N(16,5) >= 147,456, improving 29,621 and 132,496. The abstract states the construction was 'discovered through interaction with ChatGPT via its standard web interface' and that 'the search was conducted without an external orchestration layer'. Discarded: this is the degree/diameter problem with diameter 5, not Moore graphs of diameter 2 and degree 57. It does not touch this problem.
events.delivers: Lower bounds on N(12,5) and N(16,5) for the degree/diameter problem. No bearing on the existence of a degree-57, diameter-2 Moore graph.
events.remains: All of the question; the work does not address it.
events.direction: None for this problem.

systems.what_it_did: Discovered the construction behind the new lower bounds for N(12,5) and N(16,5). This is a different problem from the one in this record; it is recorded because the AI involvement is real, and so the later pass can judge its relevance.

events.what_happened: Afonso S. Bandeira, Dmitry Kunisky, Petar Nizic-Nikolac, Lucas Pesenti and Robert Wang, 'The Hypergraph Moore Bound', arXiv:2607.14068 (month from the identifier; the day was not found). Title and author list from the PDF metadata; the body was unreadable binary. A hypergraph analogue of the Moore bound. Discarded: an analogue on hypergraphs, not Moore graphs of degree 57. AI lead, UNVERIFIED: a search summary says the paper credits 'GPT-5.6 Sol' with finding the core technical innovation of the proof. A second fetch found no such mention, and the body was not readable, so I cannot confirm either way.
events.revisions: Identifier 2607.14068v2 seen; v1 date not verified.
events.delivers: A hypergraph version of the Moore bound, per the title. No bearing on the degree-57 graph as far as the title shows; the body was not read.
events.direction: None for this problem.

events.what_happened: Epoch AI lists 'The Missing Moore Graph' on its FrontierMath: Open Problems page as Unsolved, field Graph theory, notability 'Solid result', construction type Finite. The task is to write a strongly regular graph with parameters (3250, 57, 0, 1) to a file of 92,625 edges, which a verifier checks; the page says 'the main risk is that the missing Moore graph does not exist'. The page is dated 2026. Its BibTeX shows an access date of 12 October 2026, one day after today's date (11 October 2026). The page names no model credited with an attempt or a solution. The launch post (27 January 2026) does not mention the problem. The Epoch Brief of 31 July 2026 says the benchmark has 50 problems and 'AI has solved three so far'; the problem's own overview page lists different counts, and I saw only 10 of its 49 items. The Moore problem is not among the solved problems named in the search summaries.
events.delivers: No mathematical result. A benchmark target: the problem is posed as an open construction with an automatic verifier.
events.directly_checkable: A submitted graph would be checked by Epoch's verifier. No submission was found in the sources.
events.doubts: The access date on the BibTeX is one day after today's date, which suggests a cached or pre-dated page. Not material to the status.
events.direction: None; it poses the question rather than answering it.

disputes.summary: Credit for the result that a degree-57 Moore graph is not vertex-transitive. Makhnev and Paduchikh (2001 abstract) credit Cameron. Dalfo (2019), Ishida (2026) and the Tjapko problem page credit Higman, whose argument Ishida describes as unpublished and which extends Aschbacher's work. Not resolved here.

Two nonexistence claims, Yang and Zhu (arXiv 1910.05989, 2019) and Makhnev (arXiv 2010.13443, 2020). Faber and Keegan (arXiv 2210.09577, 2022) say the Makhnev case analysis 'seems not to be correct'. No refereed resolution of either claim was found. The Yang and Zhu argument was not read.

Search summaries attributed a nonexistence proof to Makhnev and Paduchikh (Algebra i logika 59(4), 2020). The abstract I read is about automorphisms of the same distance-regular graph and makes no nonexistence claim. Recorded as a discarded event. The same summaries also gave a 275 odd-order bound where the other sources give 375.

summary: The problem has no accepted settlement as of 11 October 2026. Wikipedia's Moore graph article, Epoch AI's FrontierMath page (Unsolved, with the main risk stated as the graph not existing), Faber and Keegan's 2022 title, Ishida's 2026 preprint and Smith and Montemanni's 2026 abstract all treat the case as open. The events since 26 January 2024 are partial. Smith and Montemanni (Symmetry, 22 November 2024) build potential t-subgraphs under a cyclic-permutation model, with 20 subgraphs against 15 previously known according to a search summary, and say that 57 would imply existence. Their Axioms paper (1 May 2026) rules out the cyclic-derangement route. Ishida (arXiv, 28 June 2026, v2 8 July 2026) proves that any such graph has no involutory automorphisms and so odd-order automorphism group; the introduction says this eliminates the even-order case. These narrow structure but do not decide existence. The close call is whether a structural restriction should count as a partial move on the problem; the question asks only about existence, so I read these as partial structure rather than progress on the question. The nonexistence claims are older: Yang and Zhu (October 2019, 'fractal block design', abstract says the graph 'does not exist') and Makhnev (26 October 2020, distance-regular graph with array {55,54,2;1,1,54} does not exist, via the Jurisic-Vidali equivalence). Neither has a journal record I found. Faber and Keegan (2022) argue Makhnev's case analysis is wrong, because the system splits into diagonal blocks each with solutions. Their objection is stated as 'seems not to be correct', not a refutation. The Yang and Zhu argument was not read, and its arXiv identifier resolves to two different papers depending on the URL; I used the title and abstract shown at the v1 page and took the month from the identifier. Older structural results (Hoffman-Singleton 1960; Damerell and Bannai-Ito 1973; the Aschbacher, Cameron and Higman exclusions; Makhnev-Paduchikh 2001; Mačaj-Širáň 2010 with bounds 375 and 110; Ducey 2015; Renteln 2020; Dalfó 2019; Smith and Montemanni 2023 heuristic evidence) are recorded as events. AI involvement: no system is credited with any mathematics on this problem in any event. The only AI-credited work I found (Mizuno, June 2026, ChatGPT) is about the degree/diameter problem at diameter 5 and is recorded as discarded. A hypergraph Moore-bound paper (July 2026) carries an unverified search-summary attribution to 'GPT-5.6 Sol' and is a different question. Epoch's problem page names no model credited with an attempt. The solver in Smith and Montemanni's 2024 work is Google OR-Tools CP-SAT, a constraint solver that I have not recorded as an AI system. Several primary sources returned 403 or unreadable binary (the Axioms and Symmetry PDFs and pages, the EURO Journal page, the Ishida PDF, the Yang and Zhu full text, the Renteln PDF, the Dalfo DOI redirect), so the details of those events rest on search summaries, which are flagged in each event.
competing_reading: If the Yang and Zhu (2019) or Makhnev (2020) argument is sound, the question was settled negatively before the window and the status should read 'resolved, no' rather than 'open'. Faber and Keegan's objection is only that the case analysis seems wrong, and I did not read Makhnev's case analysis to check it. Conversely, a reader could count Ishida's result as a substantial partial result: it removes the entire even-order branch, so any remaining graph must have odd-order automorphism group, which the 375 bound then limits. That is progress on structure, not on existence, which is what the statement asks.
what_would_settle_it: (1) Journal publication, or a published refutation, of arXiv 2010.13443 and arXiv 1910.05989. For Makhnev, the test is the case analysis that Faber and Keegan dispute. For Yang and Zhu, the first step is resolving the arXiv identifier conflict and then reading the argument. (2) An explicit strongly regular graph with parameters (3250, 57, 0, 1), which can be checked by counting its 92,625 edges, or an accepted nonexistence proof. (3) Refereed publication of Ishida (2026) and of the 2026 Smith and Montemanni paper, and any expert commentary on them. (4) Reading the full text of the Smith and Montemanni papers (Symmetry 2024, Axioms 2026, EURO Journal 2023), which I could not open, to confirm their claims and their statements, if any, about computer or AI assistance.

event.what_happened: Yawara Ishida, 'No involutions in the missing Moore graph', arXiv:2606.29183, math.CO; single author; affiliation given as 'A.I. System Research, Inc., Kyoto, Japan'. v1 Sunday 28 June 2026; v2 8 July 2026 (current). Theorem 1.1 (per the HTML fetch): a Moore graph of diameter two and degree 57 has no automorphism of order 2, so its automorphism group has odd order (Corollary 6.1). The introduction says the main result 'eliminates the even-order case altogether'. Method (abstract): a trace-rank identity from Brauer quotients of p-permutation lattices, applied to the 2-adic summand for eigenvalue -8, giving a contradiction. Read: the arXiv abstract page and the HTML version (first 100,000 of 100,069 characters). The PDF returned unreadable binary.
event.revisions: v1 28 Jun 2026; v2 8 Jul 2026 (current). v1 and v2 differences not examined.
event.delivers: Structural only: any degree-57 Moore graph has odd-order automorphism group, with no involutions. This removes the even-order branch that the 110 bound (Mačaj-Širáň) and the Makhnev-Paduchikh route had covered. It does not establish existence or nonexistence.
event.remains: Existence. The odd-order case, which keeps the 375 bound, is also open.
event.direction: A restriction on symmetry of any hypothetical graph, which narrows structure without deciding existence.

events.credibility_reason: Claimed landmark nonexistence proof with no journal publication or uptake in about 7 years; Wikipedia, Epoch, Ishida (2026) and Smith-Montemanni (2026) all still call the problem open; arXiv identity of the paper itself is confused.
events.direction: refuted

events.credibility_reason: Faber and Keegan (2022) identify a specific flaw in the key case analysis (the equation system splits into small diagonal blocks that all have solutions); no answer found, never published, and later work treats the problem as open.
events.direction: refuted

judgement.why: The statement asks only whether the degree-57 Moore graph exists. Structural constraints on a hypothetical graph (automorphism bounds, critical group, adjacency constraints, partial t-subgraphs) settle no restriction of the existence question and are scored none; the 2026 cyclic-derangement result rules out a construction method, not a class of graphs, so it is none (F4). The close call is Ishida (2026): proving no such graph has an involutory automorphism settles nonexistence within a class of objects (graphs with even-order automorphism group), which I score as case, in the same way as the pre-snapshot vertex-transitivity/rank-3 exclusions; direction is left null because the statement is a question, not a conjecture with an expected answer. Makhnev's 2020 nonexistence claim carries a specific, unanswered objection to its key case analysis and is knocked down; Yang-Zhu has no uptake for seven years while every later source calls the problem open, so not credible. Mizuno is a different problem (degree/diameter at diameter 5) and Bandeira et al. a hypergraph analogue: variants. Mizuno's ChatGPT construction is generated for that event only; the Bandeira AI lead is unverified and has no systems entry, so none. Journal publications are scored digested as journals of record. The Epoch listing's year-only 2026 date cannot be placed against 26 January.
judgement.doubts: Ishida's case scope is a judgement call: a reader could treat 'no involutions' as a structural constraint (none) rather than a settled class. Ishida is unreviewed, single-author, from an outfit named 'A.I. System Research, Inc.'; the final 69 HTML characters (possibly acknowledgements) were not read, so an AI disclosure cannot be ruled out. Smith-Montemanni 2024/2026 details rest on search summaries (pages 403).
